sections.body:
Sharing means letting somebody else have a turn with a toy you like. Taking turns means one child uses it first, and the next child uses it after that.

Every child wants the best toy in the room. That is normal. When you think about losing it, your hands feel tight and your tummy feels hot. Your voice gets loud too.

Sharing is not the same as giving your favourite toy away forever. Sharing is taking turns. You get the toy back later.

Children who learn to share early find playing easier. They wait less. They say yes more often. They get invited to more games, and they make more friends.

Sharing is a skill you practise, like tying your shoes. Nobody is born knowing how to do it. Some children learn it in a week. Some take a whole year. Both are fine.

The first thing you need is a word for the feeling. When you can say "I am cross because I want that", the feeling gets a little smaller. Small feelings are easier to handle than big ones.
examples: Can I have a turn after you?
I will be the next one.
sections.heading: What sharing and taking turns mean

sections.body:
When you hold a good toy, it feels like giving it away. That feeling is strong, and it is not a bad feeling. Your brain likes what it has. When you think of sharing, your brain pictures an empty hand.

Here is the other side. When you share, you get something back too. You learn what your friend likes. You get a turn when you need one. Your friend thinks you are nice, and nice children get asked to play.

Words help your body calm down. When you say the words out loud, your hands relax and your voice goes back to normal.

Sometimes you feel afraid to ask. You think your friend will say no. So you grab the toy instead. But grabbing makes everybody sad. Nobody feels good after a grab.

Try this instead. Say the sentence. Wait for the answer. If the answer is no, your turn will come. You can ask again another time.

Waiting is hard for everybody. Adults find it hard too. That is why grown-ups get cross in queues. Your turn will come, and the wait is not forever.
examples: Please can I have a turn?
I can wait until you finish.
sections.heading: Why sharing feels hard at first

sections.body:
Sharing goes much better when you follow the same steps every time. Here they are.

First, look at the toy. Name the feeling in your body. It might be cross, excited or worried.

Second, say the words out loud. Use a friendly voice, not a sharp one.

Third, ask for the turn. "Can I play with it after you?" is easy to say and easy to answer.

Fourth, wait. Look at the clock, or count to twenty in your head. Do not grab while you wait.

Fifth, when your turn comes, take it. Then say thank you. Thanking makes the next wait easy for the other child.

If your friend says no, step four gets longer. Wait for another time. A toy that is finished is often free again.

Practice makes this quicker. The tenth time you ask, your words come out much faster than the first time.
examples: I feel cross because I want that toy.
Can I have a turn when you finish?
Thank you for letting me play.
sections.heading: How to share a toy, step by step
steps: Look at the toy and name the feeling.
Say the words out loud in a friendly voice.
Take your turn and say thank you.

sections.body:
These are the words you need when you play with other children. Learn them and you can ask for what you want.

A **share** is when you let somebody else use your toy, and you use it later.

Take turns means playing first and then playing next. It is the same idea as sharing, but it has a time in it.

Waiting means doing something else while it is not your turn. It does not mean standing still and sighing.

Trade means you give one thing and you get another thing back. Trading is sharing with a swap.

Try saying each word out loud while you play. Words stick when you use them with your hands.
examples: Can I share this with you?
It is your turn, then it is mine.
sections.heading: The sharing words, one by one

terms.example: I share my cars with my friend.
terms.gloss: To let somebody else use your toy, and to get it back later.

terms.example: We take turns on the slide.
terms.gloss: To play first and then let the next person play.

terms.example: I wait until my friend finishes the puzzle.
terms.gloss: To stay calm and do something else until your turn comes.

terms.example: I trade my ball for your dinosaur.
terms.gloss: To give one thing away and get a different thing back.

sections.body:
Sometimes sharing does not work out, and that is alright. Here is what to do.

If a small child grabs your toy, do not grab back. Say the words again, close to them: "I am using this now. I will give it to you next." Then wait. Grown-ups can help you if the grabbing goes on.

If you want something back, ask for it back. "Please give my car back" is a better sentence than pulling your hand in.

If the toy is broken or special, you do not have to share it. Some things are only for you. Say so kindly: "This one is mine, but you can use my other car."

If sharing feels too big today, you can ask an adult to help you talk to your friend. That is not cheating. Grown-ups do this too.

And sometimes sharing is easy. You give your friend a piece and they give you one back. Both of you walk away smiling. That is the good feeling at the end of the wait.
examples: I am using this now. You can have it next.
This one is mine, but you can use my other car.
sections.heading: When sharing still feels too hard

sections.body:
Some children think sharing means giving your things to other children for good. It does not.

Sharing means taking turns. If a friend plays with your car, you play with it next. If you lend your picture book, you read it next.

You can say no sometimes. You can say "not now" and "not this one". A friendly no is better than a cross yes.

Here is a nice way to think about it. Your toys are yours. Sharing is a gift you give, not a thing you must give.

And when you share, you get good things too. You learn new games. You hear new stories. You find out who is a real friend. Sharing is a way of making more room for yourself, not less.
examples: You can have it next, when my turn is over.
Not now, but you can have it later.
I will share with you, and you can share with me.
sections.heading: Sharing is not giving everything away

item.summary: Sharing feels hard at first, and it gets easier with practice. After reading this, you can name the feeling, ask for a turn in words, wait your turn calmly, and keep a toy that is truly yours.
item.title: Learning to Share and Take Turns
